name: Omar Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for meeting me, Omar. I work for the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no links to any company, union, party or government, and nothing you say will carry your name. Could you describe a normal working day for me?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work at Delgado & Sons, a family agency on the high street in the town where I grew up, and I've been there a year and a half. Mr Delgado, Rui, is a friend of my father's, and he took me on after I spent six years at my uncle's tyre shop. My day is answering the phone, which rings all day because our customers are older and they like to call, then viewings, then helping Rui with valuations. I'm still learning; last month I priced a terrace 10,000 too high and it sat for eight weeks, and Rui made me ring the owner every Friday to apologise.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm engaged to Lucia, who's a receptionist at the dentist on Mill Street, and the wedding's next September at St Joseph's, where we both go. I rent a flat, and she lives with her parents until the wedding. We've got about three months' worth saved between us, plus what we've put aside for the reception.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here's the first picture. It's called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Good. I'll be honest, I'd be pleased.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I always thought it was mostly talk. At work I'd tell Rui we were right not to spend money on all those systems. With the lads after Mass I'd say people should get back to proper work and stop staring at screens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd be relieved, because I've never used any of it and I don't want to. Our business is people who've known Rui, the owner, for forty years. My job's safe as long as I learn to price properly and keep the phone answered.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going exactly as I am and work on my valuations, going out with Rui every time he lets me. I'd keep putting 250 a month toward the wedding and the deposit. And I'd stay off all the AI stuff, same as now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Happy, really. Like the storm went round us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is there anything that worries you even in that world?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Money, a little. The wedding's going to cost about 12,000 with everything, and Lucia's parents are paying a share, which I feel bad about. I'd like to be the one paying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would Rui say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: He'd say good, now go and sell the Hendersons' bungalow. He's not a man for speeches. He's sixty-four and he's never sent an email when he could make a phone call instead.

say: I'd say AI was **mostly talk** all along.
I'd tell Rui we were right not to **spend money** on new systems.
think: I'm **relieved**; I've never used AI and don't want to.
My job's **safe** if I learn to price properly and answer the phone.
do: Go out on every **valuation** Rui allows to improve my pricing.
Keep saving **250 a month** for the wedding and a deposit.
Stay **off AI tools**, same as now.
feel: **Calm** and happy, like the storm went round us.
S0.quote: Our business is people who've known Rui, the owner, for forty years.
fieldNote: His security rests on **loyal customers** and a boss who's a family friend.
His money worry is about **pride**: Lucia's parents paying toward the wedding.
He admits a costly **pricing mistake** but sees it as learnable.

steps.text: Join Rui on every valuation to improve his pricing
Save 250 a month toward the wedding and a deposit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one I don't like the sound of.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people still want to deal with a person they can trust, and that a firm like ours is built on handshakes. At work I'd say we should carry on doing what we do well. I don't go online much, so I'd keep it to family.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think the big online agencies would get cheaper and cheaper, and our older customers would start listening to their children, who use the apps. Rui is sixty-four. If business drops he could sell to a chain, and a chain wouldn't keep a junior who doesn't use their systems.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and work harder: more viewings, more evenings. I'd cut back on the wedding: fewer guests, no band, my cousin does the photos. And I'd wait and see what Rui decides before I do anything drastic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried. A sort of tightness. I'd pray about it, honestly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd wait and see what Rui decides. Wouldn't learning the systems help you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe. But I don't trust them, and I'm slow at them. My uncle always says you don't change horses halfway across the river. I'd rather be very good at the old way than bad at the new one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you turn to if things got tight?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Family first, always. My uncle would have me back at the tyre shop tomorrow, and the parish has a men's group that helps people find work. I'd never go to the government for money if my family could help.

say: I'd say people still want a person they can **trust**, built on handshakes.
I'd tell colleagues to **carry on** doing what we do well.
think: **Online agencies** get cheaper, and older customers follow their children to the apps.
If Rui **sells to a chain**, a junior without their systems goes.
do: Work **more viewings** and evenings to keep business up.
Trim the wedding: **fewer guests**, no band, a cousin taking photos.
**Wait** for Rui's decision before doing anything drastic.
feel: **Worried** and tight, and he'd pray about it.
S1.quote: I'd rather be very good at the old way than bad at the new one.
fieldNote: He sees the threat as **cheaper online rivals**, not AI inside his own firm.
He prefers **old skills** to new tools, quoting his uncle about horses mid-river.
His safety net is **family and parish**, never government money.

steps.text: Take more viewings and evening appointments
Cut the wedding guest list and drop the band
Wait for Rui's decision on the business before acting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two years. God help us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is going too fast and nobody asked ordinary people. At church I'd say we need to look after each other, like we always have. At work I'd tell Rui we'd stand by him.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think Delgado & Sons is finished within a year of it arriving. The pricing, the paperwork, the adverts: all thinking work, and a computer does it for nothing in 2028. People would still want someone to show them round until the robots come in 2031, but the online firms would send a cheap stranger, not pay me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd go back to my uncle's tyre shop, because changing tyres and fixing brakes is hands-on and it lasts at least until 2031. I'd ask Lucia if we should move the wedding forward and keep it small, and move in with her parents for a while to save. And I'd lean on the parish men's group for any work going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened. Ashamed, a bit, to go backwards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why ashamed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my father was proud when the estate agency took me on in a shirt and tie, and going back to the tyre shop feels like I failed. But my father worked a lathe for thirty years and nobody calls that failing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you and Lucia talk about that night?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Whether we still try for children soon. Lucia wants three. I'd say yes, still, because what's the point of any of this without a family, but we'd have to do it on tyre-shop wages.

say: I'd say it's going **too fast** and nobody asked ordinary people.
At church I'd urge we **look after each other**; at work I'd stand by Rui.
think: Delgado & Sons is **finished** within a year; pricing and paperwork go in 2028.
Until robots in 2031, online firms would send a **cheap stranger** for viewings.
do: Go back to **my uncle's tyre shop**, hands-on work that lasts past 2031.
Move the **wedding forward**, keep it small, and live with Lucia's parents to save.
Ask the **parish men's group** about any work going.
feel: **Frightened**, and a little **ashamed** to go backwards.
S2.quote: My father was proud when the estate agency took me on in a shirt and tie, and going back to the tyre shop feels like I failed.
fieldNote: He sees that **valuation** is thinking work and the firm's core.
The **tyre shop** is a family fallback, but it stings his pride.
Family plans hold: he'd still want **children** on tyre-shop wages.

steps.text: Return to his uncle's tyre shop fixing tyres and brakes
Bring the wedding forward and keep it small
Move in with Lucia's parents for a while to save
Ask the parish men's group for any work going

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years. That's a bit of time, at least.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we've got a few years to look after our own, and families and churches should get ready. At work I'd tell Rui we should hold on to the customers who trust us. I'd stay away from the online arguments.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd still lose this job, probably around 2031 when the computers can price a house. But five years gives me time to do it properly: learn the mechanics side with my uncle, maybe take over the shop one day, since his sons don't want it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay with Rui two more years and spend Saturdays at the tyre shop learning brakes and alignment. We'd have the wedding as planned but save hard after, 300 a month. And I'd talk to my uncle about buying into the shop slowly, so it's mine one day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but better. Like there's a road, even if it's not the one I wanted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Doesn't the tyre shop face robots too, by 2034?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe, but every car in my uncle's tyre shop is different, and half of them are older than me. I'd bet on hands for a while longer. And if the robots come, at least it's a business I'd own.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would Lucia support that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Lucia would say whatever keeps us near family. Her dad ran a bakery for twenty years. She understands small business better than I do.

say: I'd say families and churches should use the **few years** to prepare.
I'd tell Rui to hold on to **loyal customers** who trust us.
think: I'd still lose this job **around 2031**, when computers can price a house.
Five years lets me learn the trade and maybe **take over the shop**.
do: Spend **Saturdays** at the tyre shop learning brakes and alignment.
Keep the wedding as planned, then save **300 a month**.
Buy into **my uncle's shop** slowly so it's mine one day.
feel: **Worried** but steadier, with a road ahead.
S3.quote: Every car in my uncle's tyre shop is different, and half of them are older than me.
fieldNote: Five years turns a fallback into a **business plan**.
He trusts varied **hands-on** car work to outlast robots for a while.
His **traditional** view shows in choosing family business over training schemes.

steps.text: Spend Saturdays at the tyre shop learning brakes and alignment
Save 300 a month after the wedding
Buy a stake in his uncle's tyre shop bit by bit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years. I'd be 37, with children, God willing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long time and good people will adapt. At church I'd say keep faith and keep working. At work I'd say nothing much; we'd just carry on.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd probably keep the agency job for a good while and still have time to switch. What bothers me is the children: what do I tell a boy in 2036 to train for? I'd want them to learn a trade, like my father did.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at Delgado & Sons and try to get good enough to do valuations by myself. We'd buy a small house in the next three years, near Lucia's parents. And I'd learn the tyre shop side slowly, a few Saturdays a month, as a backup.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but mostly at peace. It's far enough away to plan for.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You'd still avoid AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Probably, yes, unless Rui told me to use them. I'm not against people using them. I just don't think I need a computer to tell me a bungalow needs a new roof.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your children to do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Learn something with your hands and stay near your family. That's what got my father through two factory closures. A screen can't fix a brake.

say: I'd say **ten years** is long and good people will adapt.
At church I'd urge people to **keep faith** and keep working.
think: I'd keep the agency job **a good while** and still have time to switch.
The real worry is what my **children** should train for.
do: Get good enough to do **valuations alone** at Delgado & Sons.
Buy a **small house** near Lucia's parents within three years.
Learn the **tyre shop** trade a few Saturdays a month as backup.
S4.quote: I just don't think I need a computer to tell me a bungalow needs a new roof.
fieldNote: With ten years his worry shifts to his **future children**.
He stays **resistant** to AI tools unless his boss insists.
His advice is **trades and family**, drawn from his father's factory closures.

steps.text: Practise valuations until Rui lets him do them alone
Buy a small house near Lucia's parents within three years
Work a few Saturdays a month at the tyre shop as backup

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028, because there's no time to do anything properly; you just grab whatever's nearest. What would help is firms and families working together, like apprenticeships where an older tradesman takes on a young man and the government helps with the wage. Not handouts; work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask about faith. A lot of people in my town would get through this through church, not through apps or the government. When my father lost his job in 2009, the parish fed us for three months, and I haven't forgotten it.

headlineQuote: When my father lost his job in 2009, the parish fed us for three months, and I haven't forgotten it.
portrait: Omar is a **27-year-old junior negotiator** at a family-run agency in his home town, engaged to Lucia.
He's **traditional** and churchgoing, trusts handshakes, and has **never used** AI tools.
He blames **cheap online agencies** more than AI, and turns to family before government.
His fallback is his **uncle's tyre shop**, which stings his pride but offers hands-on work.
With more time he plans to **buy into** that shop and raise a family nearby.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because there's no time to do anything **properly**.
whatWouldHelp: **Apprenticeships** where an older tradesman trains a young man, with help on wages.
**Work, not handouts**, backed by family and church.
